attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his Substack post, written in his own voice. He is not quoting anyone else.

semantics.note: Restates both clauses and keeps 'a lot', 'many' and 'seem'. 'Seem' describes how lawyers appear, not a probability hedge, so this is a present-tense observation.

contract.note: A fair, ordinary plain reading. It needs brief-specific use plus reported reactions of apparent shock, and treats neither phrase as meaning a majority. The May 2025 window follows the post's own context. Thin evidence is not counted as contradiction.

evidence.note: Survey released before the target period. It combines briefs with memos and does not measure reactions, so it is background only.
Court record from May 2025: a lawyer said she was shocked when her cited cases could not be found. This is one instance and does not show 'many'.
May 2025 report of ChatGPT-made citations in court filings. It records apologies and acknowledged limits, not shock. It neither establishes nor rules out how widespread shock was.
2026 tribunal ruling, available before the cutoff. It found the e2 lawyer used ChatGPT and misled the court, which undercuts her account. It does not settle whether shock was widespread.

reviews.rationale: Nothing in the packet measures how many lawyers used these tools for briefs specifically in May 2025. Only one documented instance of apparent shock is present (e2), and later findings cast doubt on it (e4). The other incident shows apologies, not shock. The evidence does not show 'many' shocked lawyers, and nothing shows that shock was rare. The outcome is unresolved.
